decisive_metrics.name: Order backlog
decisive_metrics.why_it_decides: The backlog is next year's revenue already signed. It is the only figure here that says whether the mix shift survives a weak order year.

decisive_metrics.name: Service revenue against last year
decisive_metrics.why_it_decides: Service is the recurring, higher-margin half. Whether it keeps outgrowing new pumps decides whether the rating should rise.

decisive_metrics.name: Free cash flow after capital spending
decisive_metrics.why_it_decides: Pumps are made in owned plants, so growth costs cash. Cash after that spending is what the owner can actually have.

what_is_changing.statement: INVENTED FIXTURE - Service is growing faster than new pumps: service revenue rose from 500.0 to 570.0 million dollars while new-pump revenue rose from 900.0 to 930.0. Service is sold on multi-year contracts, so the revenue that arrives next year is largely already signed, and it carries a higher margin than the pump it attaches to. The mix is shifting toward the recurring half of the business, which is why the backlog matters more to this question than the quarter's revenue does.

EXMP.what_it_does: INVENTED FIXTURE - Example Manufacturing builds industrial pumps and sells the service contracts that keep them running. Its customers are water utilities, mines and chemical plants, which buy a pump to move fluid they cannot afford to stop moving. If the company vanished, a customer would have to re-engineer its fluid handling around another maker's pump and re-qualify it on a live site, which takes about a year, and would have to find spare parts and service crews elsewhere in the meantime.

tier2.text: INVENTED FIXTURE - Three makers supply most of this class of industrial pump: Example Manufacturing at 28 percent of units sold, Pump Makers Corp at 24 percent and Valve Industries at 11 percent, with the rest split among about 40 regional builders. Example wins re-orders on its service network - 42 depots against Pump Makers Corp's 19 - because a stopped pump costs a mine more per day than the pump itself. A utility that buys nothing keeps its existing units and rebuilds them on a seven-year cycle, and every bid is priced against that alternative.
